title: Phishing: spot the bait before you bite
subtitle: How attackers get people to hand over the keys, and how to catch them before you do.

cards.title: You first
cards.say: I can't protect anyone while my own accounts are wide open. Neither can you. So we start with yours.

rules.headline: Read the domain after the @.
rules.body: Letter by letter. thisistea.example and thisistae-app.example don't have the same owner.

rules.headline: Notice the rush.
rules.body: A two-hour deadline is a worry someone else planted in you. It proves nothing.

rules.headline: Never type a password after clicking an email link.
rules.body: Open the site yourself: from a bookmark, or by typing the address.

cards.sign_off: I do trust people. Once I've checked.

cards.title: Protect the whole house
cards.say: One badly shut door and the water gets into every room. I've seen it happen more than once. Your inbox is one of those doors. Keep an eye on it and you protect your colleagues too, a bit like a vaccine protects the people around you.

rules.headline: Confirm the unusual with a second person.
rules.body: A transfer, a password reset, an "urgent" file: check through another channel. A phone call takes a minute.

rules.headline: Tell your colleagues.
rules.body: If a strange email reached you, it has probably reached them too. Report it to the IT team so we can warn everyone.

rules.headline: A second lock for the whole team.
rules.body: With multi-factor authentication, a stolen password becomes a nuisance rather than a break-in.

cards.sign_off: The strong teams I've known weren't extraordinary. They'd simply got into the habit of warning each other.

sections.intro: Hello! I've seen hundreds of dodgy links go by, and I never check one alone. Here's my crew: four free tools that work for you.

tools.name: Bitwarden
tools.what: Free, open-source password manager, for you and for your team.
tools.dog_says: My oldest companion. He remembers all your passwords and only offers your login on the site whose address matches. On a copy he offers nothing, and that silence is your warning.

tools.name: VirusTotal
tools.what: Runs a link or file past more than 70 scanning engines at once.
tools.dog_says: Right-click the link, choose "Copy link address", then paste it here. The time to ask is before the click.

tools.name: URLScan.io
tools.what: Opens the page remotely, in its own browser, and shows you a screenshot.
tools.dog_says: He walks down the dark alley for you. You see where the link leads, and he's the one taking the risk.

tools.name: Have I Been Pwned
tools.what: Tells you whether your email address shows up in a known data breach.
tools.dog_says: Wondering where Spider found your address? Type it in here. Then change your password on every site that appears in the list.

hunt.intro: This email hides three tricks. Click anything that looks rigged to you. And don't count on me to tell you whether you're getting warm...

flags.title: The address
flags.spider_says: Two letters swapped, one word added. Under stress, who takes the time to read every letter?

flags.title: The countdown
flags.spider_says: I wrote "within 2 hours" and panic did the rest. It sends the part of you that checks to sleep.

flags.title: The ask
flags.spider_says: ThisIsTea will never ask for your password by email. I will. All I had to do was look like them.

hunt.debrief: The three tricks Spider just bragged about are my three rules: address, rush, password. Read them through once more.

recovery.title_caught: If a real one ever catches you, here's what to do.
recovery.lead_caught: This was an exercise: nothing was stolen. Real traps catch careful people too, and then what counts is how quickly the door gets shut. Here are the steps.
recovery.title_default: Keep this plan close to hand
recovery.lead_default: This one didn't get you. Some day a better-made one will come along. Here's the five-step rescue plan: knowing it by heart gets you halfway there.

steps.headline: Change the password, on the real site.
steps.body: Open the site yourself, from a bookmark or by typing the address, never from the email. Then change that password everywhere you reused it.

steps.headline: Turn on multi-factor authentication.
steps.body: With a second lock, a stolen password is no longer enough to open the door.

steps.headline: Tell the IT team or security straight away.
steps.body: If you can, forward the email as an attachment. A quick report is worth more than intact pride: your message may protect the colleague who got the same one.

steps.headline: Look for unusual activity.
steps.body: Check your sign-in history and the list of connected devices. Make sure no mail rule is forwarding or deleting your messages. Sign out anything you don't recognise.

steps.headline: Expect a second attempt.
steps.body: Attackers often come back with a message that refers to the first one. Stay on your guard for the next few weeks.

levels.label: Not there yet
levels.reply: Nothing unusual about that. Nobody learns this in one sitting. Read Cat's three rules again, then try one of Dog's tools on a link. We'll get there together, at your pace.

levels.label: Getting there
levels.reply: Good. Keep that reflex. The next trick won't look like this one.

levels.label: Confident
levels.reply: Confident? Charming. That's my favourite audience... I'll write to you soon.

sections.prompt: Fancy a real test? We'll send **one practice phishing email** to {{email}} at a random moment in the next few minutes. It will look like a real scam, but it's harmless and will never ask for a password. Your job is to spot it.
sections.done: On its way. Watch your inbox, and use the four steps.
